title: Ezekiel 16:53–63
context: The allegory ends with an unexpected promise. The LORD says he will reverse the captivity of Sodom, Samaria, and Jerusalem, and restore each to their former estate, so that Jerusalem will bear her shame and stop boasting. Although Jerusalem despised the oath and broke the covenant, the LORD will remember his covenant made in her youth and establish an everlasting covenant with her (compare Ezekiel 37:26). When he has forgiven all she has done, she will remember, be ashamed, and never again open her mouth in pride. Both traditions read this as shared ground about mercy after shame. On the new covenant theme, see the Hebrews 8:10 note.

verses.text: “ ‘ “I will reverse their captivity, the captivity of Sodom and her daughters, and the captivity of Samaria and her daughters, and the captivity of your captives among them;
verses.arminianNotes: “I will reverse their captivity.” Arminian readers see the surprising promise of restoration for Sodom and Samaria as well as Jerusalem, revealing the LORD's mercy beyond expectation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that restoring Sodom is startling, since Sodom had been destroyed. Interpreters differ on whether to read it as a future restoration of places, of peoples, or as a rhetorical shaming of Jerusalem; it is not settled here.

verses.text: that you may bear your own shame, and may be ashamed because of all that you have done, in that you are a comfort to them.
verses.arminianNotes: “that you may bear your own shame.” Arminian readers see the purpose of the restoration: Jerusalem will see her sin clearly and be humbled, “in that you are a comfort to them.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Jerusalem's comfort to her sisters lay in her worse sins, which made them look better. Restoration comes with humbling, not pride, a point both traditions share.

verses.text: Your sisters, Sodom and her daughters, will return to their former estate; and Samaria and her daughters will return to their former estate; and you and your daughters will return to your former estate.
verses.arminianNotes: “Your sisters, Sodom and her daughters, will return to their former estate.” Arminian readers see restoration extended equally to all three sisters, so that Jerusalem stands on the same level as those she despised.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel phrasing, which puts Jerusalem beside Sodom and Samaria. Mercy removes every ground for Jerusalem's boasting over the others.

verses.text: For your sister Sodom was not mentioned by your mouth in the day of your pride,
verses.arminianNotes: “For your sister Sodom was not mentioned by your mouth in the day of your pride.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem's past contempt: in her pride she would not even speak of Sodom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse may describe either silence or scorn toward Sodom. Either way, it exposes Jerusalem's pride, which the coming restoration will humble.

verses.text: before your wickedness was uncovered, as at the time of the reproach of the daughters of Syria, and of all who are around her, the daughters of the Philistines, who despise you all around.
verses.arminianNotes: “before your wickedness was uncovered.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem's pride lasting until her sin was exposed, and her neighbors, Syria and the Philistines, now despise her.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the reproach of the surrounding nations becomes part of Jerusalem's shame. The text does not specify the occasion, and one is not supplied here.

verses.text: You have borne your lewdness and your abominations,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Jerusalem has borne her abominations. Arminian readers see him stating that she bears the consequences of her sin, as the preceding verdict declared.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this verse closes the account of judgment before the final promise. Both traditions see the consequences as real and just before mercy is announced.

verses.text: “ ‘For the Lord GOD says: “I will also deal with you as you have done, who have despised the oath in breaking the covenant.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will also deal with you as you have done.” Arminian readers see the LORD treating Jerusalem according to her conduct, since she “despised the oath in breaking the covenant.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that covenant breaking is the final charge. The LORD's justice is real. The next verse begins with “Nevertheless,” marking the turn to grace.

verses.text: Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you.
verses.arminianNotes: “Nevertheless I will remember my covenant with you in the days of your youth.” Arminian readers see the LORD's faithfulness reaching beyond Jerusalem's unfaithfulness: “I will establish an everlasting covenant with you.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD's remembering contrasts with Jerusalem's forgetting in verses 22 and 43. Many connect the everlasting covenant with the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:31; on that theme, see the Hebrews 8:10 note.

verses.text: Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your sisters, your elder sisters and your younger; and I will give them to you for daughters, but not by your covenant.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed.” Arminian readers see Jerusalem receiving her sisters as daughters, a gift that comes “not by your covenant,” that is, not on the basis of her faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase “not by your covenant” stresses that the gift rests on the LORD's initiative. Interpreters differ on the exact sense, and these notes leave it open.

verses.text: I will establish my covenant with you. Then you will know that I am the LORD;
verses.arminianNotes: “I will establish my covenant with you.” Arminian readers see the LORD's covenant renewed by his own word, leading to knowledge of him: “Then you will know that I am the LORD.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD says “my covenant,” the covenant he establishes. Both traditions see the goal of knowing the LORD, the refrain that runs through Ezekiel.

verses.text: that you may remember, and be confounded, and never open your mouth any more because of your shame, when I have forgiven you all that you have done,” says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “that you may remember, and be confounded.” Arminian readers see forgiveness producing humility: Jerusalem will “never open your mouth any more because of your shame,” with gratitude rather than boasting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers compare Romans 3:19, “that every mouth may be closed.” Ezekiel 20:43 and 36:31 also join remembering with shame after restoration. Forgiveness silences boasting, a point both traditions share.
